title: Cybersecurity Data Extraction from Common Crawl
summary: Alpha-Root is a cybersecurity-focused dataset collected in a single shot from the Common Crawl web graph using community detection. Unlike iterative content-scoring approaches like DeepSeekMath, we mine quality domains directly from the web graph, starting from just 20 trusted seed domains.

AI.tldr: Alpha-Root is a cybersecurity dataset built by applying community detection on the Common Crawl web graph, identifying high-quality domains from 20 seed domains without iterative scoring.
AI.motivation: To develop a more efficient and scalable method for identifying high-quality cybersecurity-related domains without relying on iterative content analysis.
AI.method: Applied community detection to the Common Crawl web graph, starting from 20 trusted seed domains to identify clusters of related, high-quality domains.
AI.result: Successfully constructed the Alpha-Root dataset by extracting quality domains directly from the web graph structure, avoiding content-based scoring.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based community detection enables efficient, one-shot identification of trustworthy cybersecurity domains, offering an alternative to content-intensive methods.

title: An Adaptive Multichain Blockchain: A Multiobjective Optimization Approach
summary: Blockchains are widely used for secure transaction processing, but their scalability remains limited, and existing multichain designs are typically static even as demand and capacity shift. We cast blockchain configuration as a multiagent resource-allocation problem: applications and operators declare demand, capacity, and price bounds; an optimizer groups them into ephemeral chains each epoch and sets a chain-level clearing price. The objective maximizes a governance-weighted combination of normalized utilities for applications, operators, and the system. The model is modular -- accommodating capability compatibility, application-type diversity, and epoch-to-epoch stability -- and can be solved off-chain with outcomes verifiable on-chain. We analyze fairness and incentive issues and present simulations that highlight trade-offs among throughput, decentralization, operator yield, and service stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic multichain blockchain configuration framework that treats chain setup as a multiagent resource allocation problem, optimizing application and operator demands into ephemeral chains per epoch to improve scalability and adaptability.
AI.motivation: Existing blockchain systems suffer from limited scalability and static multichain architectures that cannot adapt to changing demand and capacity; this work aims to introduce dynamic, market-driven reconfiguration for better efficiency and fairness.
AI.method: Models blockchain configuration as a multiagent resource-allocation problem where applications and operators submit demands and capacity; uses an off-chain optimizer to group participants into ephemeral chains each epoch, setting clearing prices and ensuring compatibility and stability; governance-weighted utility maximization guides optimization.
AI.result: Simulations demonstrate trade-offs between throughput, decentralization, operator yield, and service stability; the approach enables higher adaptability and resource efficiency while maintaining fairness and incentive alignment.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, market-based multichain configuration improves blockchain scalability and responsiveness; the modular, verifiable design supports evolving demands and promotes balanced incentives across stakeholders.

title: Optimized Disaster Recovery for Distributed Storage Systems: Lightweight Metadata Architectures to Overcome Cryptographic Hashing Bottleneck
summary: Distributed storage architectures are foundational to modern cloud-native infrastructure, yet a critical operational bottleneck persists within disaster recovery (DR) workflows: the dependence on content-based cryptographic hashing for data identification and synchronization. While hash-based deduplication is effective for storage efficiency in steady-state operation, it becomes a systemic liability during failover and failback events when hash indexes are stale, incomplete, or must be rebuilt following a crash. This paper precisely characterizes the operational conditions under which full or partial re-hashing becomes unavoidable. The paper also analyzes the downstream impact of cryptographic re-hashing on Recovery Time Objective (RTO) compliance, and proposes a generalized architectural shift toward deterministic, metadata-driven identification. The proposed framework assigns globally unique composite identifiers to data blocks at ingestion time-independent of content analysis enabling instantaneous delta computation during DR without any cryptographic overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies cryptographic hashing as a bottleneck in disaster recovery for distributed storage and proposes a metadata-driven, deterministic identification method to enable fast, hash-free synchronization.
AI.motivation: Content-based cryptographic hashing, while useful for deduplication, creates bottlenecks in disaster recovery due to the need for re-hashing when indexes are lost or stale.
AI.method: The paper analyzes operational conditions requiring re-hashing, evaluates its impact on RTO, and proposes a deterministic, metadata-based block identification framework.
AI.result: The framework enables instantaneous delta computation during failover and failback without cryptographic overhead, improving RTO compliance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed metadata-driven approach eliminates reliance on content-based hashing, enabling faster and more reliable disaster recovery in distributed storage systems.

title: TT-SEAL: TTD-Aware Selective Encryption for Adversarially-Robust and Low-Latency Edge AI
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. This paper has been accepted at Design Automation Conference (DAC) 2026
summary: Cloud-edge AI must jointly satisfy model compression and security under tight device budgets. While Tensor-Train Decomposition (TTD) shrinks on-device models, prior selective-encryption studies largely assume dense weights, leaving its practicality under TTD compression unclear. We present TT-SEAL, a selective-encryption framework for TT-decomposed networks. TT-SEAL ranks TT cores with a sensitivity-based importance metric, calibrates a one-time robustness threshold, and uses a value-DP optimizer to encrypt the minimum set of critical cores with AES. Under TTD-aware, transfer-based threat models (and on an FPGA-prototyped edge processor) TT-SEAL matches the robustness of full (black-box) encryption while encrypting as little as 4.89-15.92% of parameters across ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and VGG-16, and drives the share of AES decryption in end-to-end latency to low single digits (e.g., 58% -> 2.76% on ResNet-18), enabling secure, low-latency edge AI.

AI.tldr: TT-SEAL is a selective-encryption framework for tensor-train compressed neural networks that securely minimizes encryption overhead by identifying and protecting only the most sensitive TT cores, enabling efficient and robust edge AI inference.
AI.motivation: Existing selective-encryption methods assume dense model weights and are not optimized for tensor-train decomposed models, creating a gap in secure and efficient edge AI deployment under tight device budgets.
AI.method: TT-SEAL introduces a sensitivity-based importance metric to rank TT cores, sets a one-time robustness threshold, and employs a value-DP optimizer to minimally encrypt critical cores using AES, under TTD-aware threat models.
AI.result: TT-SEAL encrypts only 4.89–15.92% of parameters across ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and VGG-16 while matching the robustness of full encryption, and reduces AES decryption latency share to as low as 2.76% (e.g., from 58% on ResNet-18).
AI.conclusion: TT-SEAL enables secure, low-latency edge AI by efficiently combining selective encryption with TTD-compressed models, significantly reducing encryption overhead while maintaining robustness.

title: EmpiRE-Compass: A Neuro-Symbolic Dashboard for Sustainable and Dynamic Knowledge Exploration, Synthesis, and Reuse
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, Accepted at 32nd International Working Conference on Requirements Engineering: Foundations for Software Quality
summary: Software engineering (SE) and requirements engineering (RE) face a significant increase in secondary studies, particularly literature reviews (LRs), due to the ever-growing number of scientific publications. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) exacerbates this trend by producing LRs rapidly but often at the expense of quality, rigor, and transparency. At the same time, secondary studies often fail to share underlying data and artifacts, limiting replication and reuse. This paper introduces EmpiRE-Compass, a neuro-symbolic dashboard designed to lower barriers for accessing, replicating, and reusing LR data. Its overarching goal is to demonstrate how LRs can become more sustainable by semantically structuring their underlying data in research knowledge graphs (RKGs) and by leveraging large language models (LLMs) for easy and dynamic access, replication, and reuse. Building on two RE use cases, we developed EmpiRE-Compass with a modular system design and workflows for curated and custom competency questions. The dashboard is freely available online, accompanied by a demonstration video. To manage operational costs, a limit of 25 requests per IP address per day applies to the default LLM (GPT-4o mini). All source code and documentation are released as an open-source project to foster reuse, adoption, and extension. EmpiRE-Compass provides three core capabilities: (1) Exploratory visual analytics for curated competency questions; (2) Neuro-symbolic synthesis for custom competency questions; and (3) Reusable knowledge with all queries, analyses, and results openly available. By unifying RKGs and LLMs in a neuro-symbolic dashboard, EmpiRE-Compass advances sustainable LRs in RE, SE, and beyond. It lowers technical barriers, fosters transparency and reproducibility, and enables collaborative, continuously updated, and reusable LRs

AI.tldr: EmpiRE-Compass is a neuro-symbolic dashboard that enhances sustainability, transparency, and reusability of literature reviews in software and requirements engineering by integrating research knowledge graphs and large language models.
AI.motivation: The increasing volume of literature reviews in software and requirements engineering, exacerbated by low-quality AI-generated reviews, combined with insufficient data sharing, undermines reproducibility and reuse; thus, a sustainable, transparent solution is needed.
AI.method: Development of a modular, neuro-symbolic dashboard (EmpiRE-Compass) that leverages research knowledge graphs and LLMs to support exploratory analytics, custom query synthesis, and open sharing of review data and artifacts.
AI.result: EmpiRE-Compass provides three core capabilities: (1) visual analytics for curated questions, (2) neuro-symbolic synthesis for custom queries, and (3) full openness of queries, analyses, and results; it is publicly available with open-source code and usage limitations to manage costs.
AI.conclusion: EmpiRE-Compass advances sustainable literature reviews in requirements and software engineering by integrating research knowledge graphs and large language models into a transparent, reproducible, and reusable neuro-symbolic framework.

title: Analysis of LLMs Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Attacks
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely deployed in real-world systems. Given their broader applicability, prompt engineering has become an efficient tool for resource-scarce organizations to adopt LLMs for their own purposes. At the same time, LLMs are vulnerable to prompt-based attacks. Thus, analyzing this risk has become a critical security requirement. This work evaluates prompt-injection and jailbreak vulnerability using a large, manually curated dataset across multiple open-source LLMs, including Phi, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3.2, Qwen, and Gemma variants. We observe significant behavioural variation across models, including refusal responses and complete silent non-responsiveness triggered by internal safety mechanisms. Furthermore, we evaluated several lightweight, inference-time defence mechanisms that operate as filters without any retraining or GPU-intensive fine-tuning. Although these defences mitigate straightforward attacks, they are consistently bypassed by long, reasoning-heavy prompts.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks on multiple open-source LLMs using a manually curated dataset, showing varied model behaviors and limited effectiveness of lightweight, inference-time defenses against complex prompts.
AI.motivation: Given the widespread deployment of LLMs and their vulnerability to prompt-based attacks, there is a critical need to assess security risks, especially for resource-scarce organizations relying on prompt engineering without extensive customization or fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors evaluate prompt-injection and jailbreak vulnerabilities using a large, manually curated dataset across multiple open-source LLMs (Phi, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3.2, Qwen, Gemma variants), and test several lightweight, inference-time defense filters without retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.result: Significant behavioral variation is observed across models, including refusal responses and silent non-responsiveness due to internal safety mechanisms. Lightweight defenses are effective against simple attacks but consistently bypassed by complex, long, reasoning-heavy prompts.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that while lightweight, inference-time defense mechanisms can mitigate simple prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks on LLMs, they are ineffective against more sophisticated, reasoning-heavy prompts, highlighting the need for more robust and adaptive security measures.

title: The Ethos of the PEERfect REVIEWer: Scientific Care and Collegial Welfare
comment: 13 pages, Accepted at the 32nd International Working Conference on Requirements Engineering: Foundations for Software Quality
summary: Peer review remains a cornerstone in academia, yet it frequently falls short in fostering joint progress and well-being. While peer review primarily emphasizes scientific rigor, it often lacks the empathy essential for supporting and encouraging all peers involved. In this experience report, I aim to highlight that peer review is a practice that demands both scientific care for quality and collegial welfare for the joint progress and well-being of all peers involved, including authors, co-reviewers, workshop or conference organizers, and journal editors. Drawing on my ten years of experience in academia, I propose the ethos of the PEERfect REVIEWer, grounded in the two core values: Scientific care and collegial welfare. Through reflection shaped by professional exchanges with colleagues, consideration of literature, and an examination of both self-authored and received reviews, I formulated an accompanying guideline with 16 practical recommendations to guide reviewers in their actions to achieve these two values. The ethos of the PEERfect REVIEWer and its accompanying guideline help reviewers in upholding high scientific standards and conducting peer review in a constructive, supportive, respectful, and timely manner. They demonstrate that scientific rigor and empathy are complementary forces that promote impactful peer review practice. By placing scientific care and collegial welfare at the core of peer review, this experience report reaffirms the importance of scientific rigor while also advocating for greater attention to empathy. It invites reviewers to reconsider their role not merely as gatekeepers but as partners in the academic journey of each peer involved. The PEERfect REVIEWer is both a caretaker of quality and a steward of joint progress and well-being - as truly impactful peer review practice requires scientific rigor and empathy in equal measure.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the PEERfect REVIEWer ethos, combining scientific care and collegial welfare through 16 practical recommendations, to foster a more empathetic, constructive, and rigorous peer review culture.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of empathy in peer review practices and promote a more constructive, supportive, and respectful review culture that values both scientific rigor and the well-being of all participants.
AI.method: An experience-based reflection over ten years in academia, informed by professional discussions, literature review, and analysis of personal and received peer reviews, leading to the development of a 16-item guideline.
AI.result: A dual-value framework (scientific care and collegial welfare) and a 16-point practical guideline that guide reviewers in conducting impactful, rigorous, and empathetic peer reviews.
AI.conclusion: The PEERfect REVIEWer ethos advocates for a balanced integration of scientific care and collegial welfare in peer review, redefining reviewers as partners in academic progress rather than mere gatekeepers.

title: EyeLayer: Integrating Human Attention Patterns into LLM-Based Code Summarization
comment: Accepted at the 34th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC 2026), April 12-13, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
summary: Code summarization is the task of generating natural language descriptions of source code, which is critical for software comprehension and maintenance. While large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on this task, an open question remains: can human expertise in code understanding further guide and enhance these models? We propose EyeLayer, a lightweight attention-augmentation module that incorporates human eye-gaze patterns, as a proxy of human expertise, into LLM-based code summarization. EyeLayer models human attention during code reading via a Multimodal Gaussian Mixture, redistributing token embeddings based on learned parameters (μ_i, σ_i^2) that capture where and how intensively developers focus. This design enables learning generalizable attention priors from eye-tracking data and incorporating them into LLMs seamlessly, without disturbing existing representations. We evaluate EyeLayer across diverse model families (i.e., LLaMA-3.2, Qwen3, and CodeBERT) covering different scales and architectures. EyeLayer consistently outperforms strong fine-tuning baselines across standard metrics, achieving gains of up to 13.17% on BLEU-4. These results demonstrate that human gaze patterns encode complementary attention signals that enhance the semantic focus of LLMs and transfer effectively across diverse models for code summarization.

AI.tldr: EyeLayer integrates human eye-gaze data into LLMs for code summarization via a lightweight attention module, using Gaussian mixtures to model developer focus and improving performance by up to 13.17% on BLEU-4 across diverse models.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to determine whether human expertise in code understanding—proxied by eye-gaze patterns—can enhance the performance of large language models in code summarization, a task crucial for software comprehension and maintenance.
AI.method: EyeLayer uses a Multimodal Gaussian Mixture to model human eye-gaze patterns during code reading, deriving attention priors (μ_i, σ_i^2) that redistribute token embeddings in LLMs without altering their original representations. This lightweight module is integrated into various LLMs (LLaMA-3.2, Qwen3, CodeBERT) to guide attention based on empirical human focus data.
AI.result: EyeLayer consistently outperforms strong fine-tuning baselines across multiple LLMs and metrics, achieving up to a 13.17% improvement in BLEU-4 score, indicating that human attention patterns provide complementary semantic signals that improve code summarization.
AI.conclusion: EyeLayer successfully incorporates human gaze patterns as a form of human expertise into LLM-based code summarization, demonstrating that such biologically-informed attention signals can consistently enhance model performance across diverse architectures.

title: Self-Purification Mitigates Backdoors in Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
summary: Multimodal Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) have recently emerged as a competitive alternative to their autoregressive counterparts. Yet their vulnerability to backdoor attacks remains largely unexplored. In this work, we show that well-established data-poisoning pipelines can successfully implant backdoors into MDLMs, enabling attackers to manipulate model behavior via specific triggers while maintaining normal performance on clean inputs. However, defense strategies effective to these models are yet to emerge. To bridge this gap, we introduce a backdoor defense framework for MDLMs named DiSP (Diffusion Self-Purification). DiSP is driven by a key observation: selectively masking certain vision tokens at inference time can neutralize a backdoored model's trigger-induced behaviors and restore normal functionality. Building on this, we purify the poisoned dataset using the compromised model itself, then fine-tune the model on the purified data to recover it to a clean one. Given such a specific design, DiSP can remove backdoors without requiring any auxiliary models or clean reference data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach effectively mitigates backdoor effects, reducing the attack success rate (ASR) from over 90% to typically under 5%, while maintaining model performance on benign tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DiSP, a self-purification defense framework for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models that effectively removes backdoors by selectively masking vision tokens and fine-tuning on self-purified data, achieving strong defense without clean data or external models.
AI.motivation: While Multimodal Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) are increasingly used, they remain vulnerable to data-poisoning-based backdoor attacks, and existing defense mechanisms for such models are lacking.
AI.method: DiSP leverages selective masking of vision tokens during inference to identify and neutralize backdoor triggers, uses the compromised model to self-purify the poisoned dataset, and fine-tunes the model on this purified data to recover clean behavior.
AI.result: DiSP reduces the attack success rate from over 90% to under 5% across multiple experiments while preserving performance on clean, benign inputs.
AI.conclusion: DiSP serves as an effective backdoor defense framework for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models, successfully restoring model integrity without relying on auxiliary models or clean data.

title: Contextual Memory Virtualisation: DAG-Based State Management and Structurally Lossless Trimming for LLM Agents
comment: 11 pages. 6 figures. Introduces a DAG-based state management system for LLM agents. Evaluation on 76 coding sessions shows up to 86% token reduction (mean 20%) while remaining economically viable under prompt caching. Includes reference implementation for Claude Code
summary: As large language models engage in extended reasoning tasks, they accumulate significant state -- architectural mappings, trade-off decisions, codebase conventions -- within the context window. This understanding is lost when sessions reach context limits and undergo lossy compaction. We propose Contextual Memory Virtualisation (CMV), a system that treats accumulated LLM understanding as version-controlled state. Borrowing from operating system virtual memory, CMV models session history as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with formally defined snapshot, branch, and trim primitives that enable context reuse across independent parallel sessions. We introduce a three-pass structurally lossless trimming algorithm that preserves every user message and assistant response verbatim while reducing token counts by a mean of 20% and up to 86% for sessions with significant overhead by stripping mechanical bloat such as raw tool outputs, base64 images, and metadata. A single-user case-study evaluation across 76 real-world coding sessions demonstrates that trimming remains economically viable under prompt caching, with the strongest gains in mixed tool-use sessions, which average 39% reduction and reach break-even within 10 turns. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/CosmoNaught/claude-code-cmv.

AI.tldr: Contextual Memory Virtualisation (CMV) is a system that preserves and reuses accumulated LLM context by modeling session history as a version-controlled DAG, enabling efficient, structurally lossless trimming and cross-session context sharing.
AI.motivation: Extended LLM reasoning tasks accumulate valuable context that is typically lost due to context window limits and lossy compaction; CMV aims to preserve this state efficiently.
AI.method: CMV models session history as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with snapshot, branch, and trim operations; it employs a three-pass structurally lossless trimming algorithm to remove mechanical bloat (e.g., tool outputs, base64 images) while retaining all user and assistant messages verbatim.
AI.result: The trimming algorithm achieves a mean 20% token reduction, up to 86% in high-overhead sessions, with 39% average reduction in mixed tool-use sessions; economic viability is demonstrated under prompt caching with break-even within 10 turns.
AI.conclusion: CMV enables efficient, reusable, and lossless context management for LLMs, enhancing scalability and cost-effectiveness in long-running reasoning tasks like coding.

title: A Lightweight Defense Mechanism against Next Generation of Phishing Emails using Distilled Attention-Augmented BiLSTM
summary: The current generation of large language models produces sophisticated social-engineering content that bypasses standard text screening systems in business communication platforms. Our proposed solution for mail gateway and endpoint deception detection operates in a privacy-protective manner while handling the performance requirements of network and mobile security systems. The MobileBERT teacher receives fine-tuning before its transformation into a BiLSTM model with multi-head attention which maintains semantic discrimination only with 4.5 million parameters. The hybrid dataset contains human-written messages together with LLM-generated paraphrases that use masking techniques and personalization methods to enhance modern attack resistance. The evaluation system uses five testing protocols which include human-only and LLM-only tests and two cross-distribution transfer tests and a production-like mixed traffic test to assess performance in native environments and across different distribution types and combined traffic scenarios. The distilled model maintains a weighted-F1 score difference of 1-2.5 points compared to the mixture split results of strong transformer baselines including ModernBERT, DeBERTaV3-base, T5-base, DeepSeek-R1 Distill Qwen-1.5B and Phi-4 mini while achieving 80-95\% faster inference times and 95-99\% smaller model sizes. The system demonstrates excellent performance in terms of accuracy and latency while maintaining a compact size which enables real-time filtering without acceleration hardware and supports policy-based management. The paper examines system performance under high traffic conditions and security measures for privacy protection and implementation methods for operational deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, privacy-preserving deception detection system for identifying LLM-generated social-engineering content in business communications, using a distilled BiLSTM with multi-head attention trained via a MobileBERT teacher on a hybrid human-LLM dataset, achieving competitive performance with significantly faster inference and smaller size.
AI.motivation: Rising use of sophisticated LLM-generated social-engineering attacks that evade standard text screening, combined with the need for privacy protection and low-latency performance in enterprise communication systems, motivates the development of efficient, deployable detection models.
AI.method: A MobileBERT teacher model is fine-tuned and used to distill knowledge into a smaller BiLSTM model with multi-head attention. The model is trained on a hybrid dataset of human-written and LLM-generated (paraphrased, masked, personalized) messages. Evaluation employs five protocols: human-only, LLM-only, cross-distribution transfer, and mixed production-like traffic.
AI.result: The distilled BiLSTM model achieves a weighted-F1 score within 1–2.5 points of strong transformer baselines (e.g., ModernBERT, DeBERTaV3-base, T5-base, DeepSeek-R1 Distill Qwen-1.5B, Phi-4 mini), while being 80–95% faster in inference and 95–99% smaller in size. It performs well under high-traffic conditions and supports real-time filtering without hardware acceleration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed compact model enables efficient, privacy-preserving, and accurate detection of LLM-driven deception in real-world business communication environments, offering a practical alternative to large transformers by balancing performance, size, and latency for deployment at mail gateways and endpoints.

title: XMENTOR: A Rank-Aware Aggregation Approach for Human-Centered Explainable AI in Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction
summary: Machine learning (ML)-based defect prediction models can improve software quality. However, their opaque reasoning creates an HCI challenge because developers struggle to trust models they cannot interpret. Explainable AI (XAI) methods such as LIME, SHAP, and BreakDown aim to provide transparency, but when used together, they often produce conflicting explanations that increase confusion, frustration, and cognitive load. To address this usability challenge, we introduce XMENTOR, a human-centered, rank-aware aggregation method implemented as a VS Code plugin. XMENTOR unifies multiple post-hoc explanations into a single, coherent view by applying adaptive thresholding, rank and sign agreement, and fallback strategies to preserve clarity without overwhelming users. In a user study, nearly 90% of the participants preferred aggregated explanations, citing reduced confusion and stronger support for daily tasks of debugging and review of defects. Our findings show how combining explanations and embedding them into developer workflows can enhance interpretability, usability, and trust.

AI.tldr: XMENTOR is a human-centered, rank-aware explanation aggregator for ML-based defect prediction that reduces confusion by unifying conflicting XAI outputs (e.g., LIME, SHAP) into a single coherent view, improving developer trust and usability in practice.
AI.motivation: The lack of consistency and clarity in explanations from multiple XAI methods leads to confusion, frustration, and high cognitive load for developers, undermining trust in ML-based defect prediction models.
AI.method: The authors propose XMENTOR, a rank-aware, adaptive aggregation method that combines explanations from multiple XAI techniques (e.g., LIME, SHAP, BreakDown) using thresholding, rank and sign agreement, and fallback strategies, implemented as a VS Code plugin. A user study was conducted to evaluate its effectiveness in real-world development tasks.
AI.result: In a user study, nearly 90% of participants preferred XMENTOR's aggregated explanations over individual XAI outputs, reporting reduced confusion and better support for debugging and code review tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining multiple XAI methods through a human-centered aggregation approach like XMENTOR enhances interpretability, usability, and trust in ML-based defect prediction models when integrated into developer workflows.

title: Poisoned Acoustics
summary: Training-data poisoning attacks can induce targeted, undetectable failure in deep neural networks by corrupting a vanishingly small fraction of training labels. We demonstrate this on acoustic vehicle classification using the MELAUDIS urban intersection dataset (approx. 9,600 audio clips, 6 classes): a compact 2-D convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on log-mel spectrograms achieves 95.7% Attack Success Rate (ASR) -- the fraction of target-class test samples misclassified under the attack -- on a Truck-to-Car label-flipping attack at just p=0.5% corruption (48 records), with zero detectable change in aggregate accuracy (87.6% baseline; 95% CI: 88-100%, n=3 seeds). We prove this stealth is structural: the maximum accuracy drop from a complete targeted attack is bounded above by the minority class fraction (beta). For real-world class imbalances (Truck approx. 3%), this bound falls below training-run noise, making aggregate accuracy monitoring provably insufficient regardless of architecture or attack method. A companion backdoor trigger attack reveals a novel trigger-dominance collapse: when the target class is a dataset minority, the spectrogram patch trigger becomes functionally redundant--clean ASR equals triggered ASR, and the attack degenerates to pure label flipping. We formalize the ML training pipeline as an attack surface and propose a trust-minimized defense combining content-addressed artifact hashing, Merkle-tree dataset commitment, and post-quantum digital signatures (ML-DSA-65/CRYSTALS-Dilithium3, NIST FIPS 204) for cryptographically verifiable data provenance.

title: Automating the Detection of Requirement Dependencies Using Large Language Models
summary: Requirements are inherently interconnected through various types of dependencies. Identifying these dependencies is essential, as they underpin critical decisions and influence a range of activities throughout software development. However, this task is challenging, particularly in modern software systems, given the high volume of complex, coupled requirements. These challenges are further exacerbated by the ambiguity of Natural Language (NL) requirements and their constant change. Consequently, requirement dependency detection is often overlooked or performed manually. Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in NL processing, presenting a promising avenue for requirement-related tasks. While they have shown to enhance various requirements engineering tasks, their effectiveness in identifying requirement dependencies remains unexplored. In this paper, we introduce LEREDD, an LLM-based approach for automated detection of requirement dependencies that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and In-Context Learning (ICL). It is designed to identify diverse dependency types directly from NL requirements. We empirically evaluate LEREDD against two state-of-the-art baselines. The results show that LEREDD provides highly accurate classification of dependent and non-dependent requirements, achieving an accuracy of 0.93, and an F1 score of 0.84, with the latter averaging 0.96 for non-dependent cases. LEREDD outperforms zero-shot LLMs and baselines, particularly in detecting fine-grained dependency types, where it yields average relative gains of 94.87% and 105.41% in F1 scores for the Requires dependency over the baselines. We also provide an annotated dataset of requirement dependencies encompassing 813 requirement pairs across three distinct systems to support reproducibility and future research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LEREDD, an LLM-based approach using RAG and ICL for automated detection of requirement dependencies in natural language; it outperforms baselines with high accuracy and F1 scores and contributes a labeled dataset of 813 requirement pairs for future research.
AI.motivation: Requirement dependency detection is critical in software engineering but hindered by the complexity, ambiguity, and evolving nature of natural language requirements; current practices are often manual or error-prone, and the potential of LLMs in this domain remains unexplored.
AI.method: LEREDD combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and In-Context Learning (ICL) with Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect diverse requirement dependencies directly from Natural Language (NL) requirements; it was evaluated against two state-of-the-art baselines using an annotated dataset of 813 requirement pairs across three systems.
AI.result: LEREDD achieves 0.93 accuracy and 0.84 F1 score in classifying dependent vs. non-dependent requirements, with 0.96 average F1 for non-dependent cases; it shows average relative F1 improvements of 94.87% and 105.41% over baselines for the 'Requires' dependency type.
AI.conclusion: LEREDD is an effective LLM-based approach for automated requirement dependency detection, outperforming existing baselines, especially in identifying fine-grained dependency types, and enabling reproducibility through a publicly available annotated dataset.

title: Differentially Private Truncation of Unbounded Data via Public Second Moments
summary: Data privacy is important in the AI era, and differential privacy (DP) is one of the golden solutions. However, DP is typically applicable only if data have a bounded underlying distribution. We address this limitation by leveraging second-moment information from a small amount of public data. We propose Public-moment-guided Truncation (PMT), which transforms private data using the public second-moment matrix and applies a principled truncation whose radius depends only on non-private quantities: data dimension and sample size. This transformation yields a well-conditioned second-moment matrix, enabling its inversion with a significantly strengthened ability to resist the DP noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of PMT by using penalized and generalized linear regressions. Specifically, we design new loss functions and algorithms, ensuring that solutions in the transformed space can be mapped back to the original domain. We have established improvements in the models' DP estimation through theoretical error bounds, robustness guarantees, and convergence results, attributing the gains to the conditioning effect of PMT. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets confirm that PMT substantially improves the accuracy and stability of DP models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Public-moment-guided Truncation (PMT), a method that leverages a small amount of public data to improve differential privacy by transforming private data using second-moment information, enabling more accurate and stable private model estimation.
AI.motivation: Differential privacy (DP) typically requires bounded data distributions, limiting its applicability; this work addresses the challenge of applying DP to unbounded or poorly conditioned data.
AI.method: PMT uses a public second-moment matrix to transform private data, applies truncation based on data dimension and sample size, and designs new loss functions and algorithms for penalized and generalized linear regressions that map solutions back to the original domain.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows improved error bounds, robustness, and convergence; experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate enhanced accuracy and stability of DP models using PMT.
AI.conclusion: Public-moment-guided Truncation (PMT) effectively improves the accuracy and stability of differentially private models by leveraging public second-moment information to condition the data space, enabling robust inversion and better DP estimation.

title: RepoMod-Bench: A Benchmark for Code Repository Modernization via Implementation-Agnostic Testing
summary:
The evolution of AI coding agents has shifted the frontier from simple snippet completion to autonomous repository-level engineering. However, evaluating these agents remains ill-posed in general code repository generation, where the lack of deterministic ground truth leads to ambiguous metrics. Code modernization via automated translation offers a more rigorous alternative by providing a fixed ground truth -- the source repository; yet existing benchmarks are limited to small-scale repositories and rely on language-specific unit tests visible to the agent, allowing test-driven overfitting.
  We address these limitations by introducing a benchmarking framework for repository-level code modernization built on an implementation-agnostic evaluation paradigm. This framework is instantiated through RepoMod-Bench: a benchmark of 21 real-world repositories with standardized interfaces, spanning 8 programming languages. The benchmark contains 1.6M lines of code (LOC) and 11,616 tests, with repository sizes ranging from 14 to 211K LOC. By targeting repositories with standardized interfaces, we utilize an implementation-agnostic test suite to verify functional equivalence between source and target implementations. This black-box approach ensures verification remains consistent across languages, and our environment hides all test suites from agents to prevent test-driven shortcuts. Evaluating four state-of-the-art agent configurations reveals a sharp scaling collapse: average pass rates drop from 91.3% on projects under 10K LOC to 15.3% on projects exceeding 50K LOC. These results demonstrate that autonomous modernization at scale remains a significant open challenge. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/Modelcode-ai/mcode-benchmark.

AI.tldr: RepoMod-Bench introduces a rigorous, implementation-agnostic framework for evaluating AI agents in large-scale code modernization, revealing that current agents fail to scale beyond small repositories.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation benchmarks for AI coding agents are limited to small repositories and rely on visible, language-specific unit tests, leading to test-driven overfitting and lacking scalability and generalization for repository-level code modernization.
AI.method: A benchmarking framework named RepoMod-Bench was introduced, featuring 21 real-world repositories (1.6M LOC, 8 languages) with standardized interfaces and hidden, implementation-agnostic test suites to prevent overfitting and ensure cross-language verification.
AI.result: Evaluation of four state-of-the-art agents shows a dramatic drop in performance: average pass rates fall from 91.3% on repositories under 10K LOC to 15.3% on those exceeding 50K LOC.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous code modernization at scale remains a significant open challenge, as current AI agents struggle with larger repositories despite performing well on smaller ones.

title: HubScan: Detecting Hubness Poisoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are essential to contemporary AI applications, allowing large language models to obtain external knowledge via vector similarity search. Nevertheless, these systems encounter a significant security flaw: hubness - items that frequently appear in the top-k retrieval results for a disproportionately high number of varied queries. These hubs can be exploited to introduce harmful content, alter search rankings, bypass content filtering, and decrease system performance.
  We introduce hubscan, an open-source security scanner that evaluates vector indices and embeddings to identify hubs in RAG systems. Hubscan presents a multi-detector architecture that integrates: (1) robust statistical hubness detection utilizing median/MAD-based z-scores, (2) cluster spread analysis to assess cross-cluster retrieval patterns, (3) stability testing under query perturbations, and (4) domain-aware and modality-aware detection for category-specific and cross-modal attacks. Our solution accommodates several vector databases (FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate) and offers versatile retrieval techniques, including vector similarity, hybrid search, and lexical matching with reranking capabilities.
  We evaluate hubscan on Food-101, MS-COCO, and FiQA adversarial hubness benchmarks constructed using state-of-the-art gradient-optimized and centroid-based hub generation methods. hubscan achieves 90% recall at a 0.2% alert budget and 100% recall at 0.4%, with adversarial hubs ranking above the 99.8th percentile. Domain-scoped scanning recovers 100% of targeted attacks that evade global detection. Production validation on 1M real web documents from MS MARCO demonstrates significant score separation between clean documents and adversarial content. Our work provides a practical, extensible framework for detecting hubness threats in production RAG systems.

AI.tldr: Hubscan is an open-source security scanner designed to detect hubness vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by identifying overrepresented items (hubs) in vector retrieval that can be exploited for attacks.
AI.motivation: RAG systems are vulnerable to security threats due to hubness in vector similarity search, where certain items appear disproportionately in top-k results across diverse queries, enabling malicious manipulation of content and bypassing safety filters.
AI.method: Hubscan uses a multi-detector approach: (1) statistical hubness detection via median/MAD-based z-scores, (2) cluster spread analysis, (3) stability testing under query perturbations, and (4) domain- and modality-aware detection. It supports multiple vector databases (FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate) and retrieval methods including hybrid and lexical search with reranking.
AI.result: Hubscan achieves 90% recall at 0.2% alert budget and 100% recall at 0.4% on adversarial benchmarks (Food-101, MS-COCO, FiQA), with adversarial hubs ranked above the 99.8th percentile. Domain-scoped scanning detects 100% of targeted attacks missed by global detection. Evaluation on 1M real documents (MS MARCO) shows clear separation between clean and adversarial content scores.
AI.conclusion: Hubscan provides a practical, extensible framework for identifying and mitigating hubness-based security threats in production RAG systems, supporting diverse databases and retrieval modalities while demonstrating high effectiveness in real-world and adversarial settings.

title: RandSet: Randomized Corpus Reduction for Fuzzing Seed Scheduling
comment: To Appear in ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and Applications (OOPSLA 2026)
summary:
Seed explosion is a fundamental problem in fuzzing seed scheduling, where a fuzzer maintains a huge corpus and fails to choose promising seeds. Existing works focus on seed prioritization but still suffer from seed explosion since corpus size remains huge. We tackle this from a new perspective: corpus reduction, i.e., computing a seed corpus subset. However, corpus reduction could lead to poor seed diversity and large runtime overhead. Prior techniques like cull_queue, AFL-Cmin, and MinSet suffer from poor diversity or prohibitive overhead, making them unsuitable for high-frequency seed scheduling.
  We propose RandSet, a novel randomized corpus reduction technique that reduces corpus size and yields diverse seed selection simultaneously with minimal overhead. Our key insight is introducing randomness into corpus reduction to enjoy two benefits of a randomized algorithm: randomized output (diverse seed selection) and low runtime cost. Specifically, we formulate corpus reduction as a set cover problem and compute a randomized subset covering all features of the entire corpus. We then schedule seeds from this small, randomized subset rather than the entire corpus, effectively mitigating seed explosion.
  We implement RandSet on three popular fuzzers: AFL++, LibAFL, and Centipede, and evaluate it on standalone programs, FuzzBench, and Magma. Results show RandSet achieves significantly more diverse seed selection than other reduction techniques, with average subset ratios of 4.03% and 5.99% on standalone and FuzzBench programs. RandSet achieves a 16.58% coverage gain on standalone programs and up to 3.57% on FuzzBench in AFL++, triggers up to 7 more ground-truth bugs than the state-of-the-art on Magma, while introducing only 1.17%-3.93% overhead.

AI.tldr: RandSet is a randomized corpus reduction technique for fuzzing that reduces seed corpus size while maintaining diversity and low overhead, effectively addressing seed explosion and improving coverage and bug detection.
AI.motivation: Seed explosion leads to inefficient seed scheduling in fuzzing; existing prioritization methods do not reduce corpus size, and current reduction techniques suffer from poor diversity or high overhead.
AI.method: RandSet formulates corpus reduction as a randomized set cover problem to compute a small, diverse subset of seeds that covers all features of the original corpus, and schedules seeds from this subset.
AI.result: RandSet achieves average subset ratios of 4.03% and 5.99% on standalone and FuzzBench programs, 16.58% coverage gain on standalone programs, up to 3.57% on FuzzBench, detects up to 7 more bugs on Magma, with only 1.17%-3.93% runtime overhead.
AI.conclusion: RandSet effectively mitigates seed explosion in fuzzing by enabling corpus reduction with high seed diversity and minimal runtime overhead, outperforming existing techniques in coverage and bug detection.

title: Predicting Known Vulnerabilities from Attack Descriptions Using Sentence Transformers
comment: PhD thesis, Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, 2026
summary:
Modern infrastructures rely on software systems that remain vulnerable to cyberattacks. These attacks frequently exploit vulnerabilities documented in repositories such as MITRE's Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE). However, Cyber Threat Intelligence resources, including MITRE ATT&CK and CVE, provide only partial coverage of attack-vulnerability relationships. Attack information often appears before vulnerabilities are formally linked, creating the need for automated methods that infer likely vulnerabilities directly from attack descriptions.
  This thesis addresses the problem of predicting known vulnerabilities from natural-language descriptions of cyberattacks. We develop transformer-based sentence embedding methods that encode attack and vulnerability descriptions into semantic vector representations, enabling similarity-based ranking and recommendation.
  Fourteen state-of-the-art transformer models were evaluated across four attack description types (Tactic, Technique, Procedure, and Attack Pattern). Results show that Technique descriptions in MITRE ATT&CK provide the strongest predictive signal. The multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1 (MMPNet) model achieved the best performance due to its hybrid pre-training and optimization for semantic similarity.
  The approach was implemented in the VULDAT tool, which automatically links attacks to vulnerabilities. Manual validation revealed previously undocumented relationships in MITRE repositories. Evaluation on unseen cyberattack reports demonstrates that the models generalize beyond curated datasets and support proactive vulnerability awareness.

AI.tldr: This thesis proposes a transformer-based approach to predict known vulnerabilities from natural-language cyberattack descriptions by leveraging semantic similarity, achieving strong performance with the MMPNet model and enabling discovery of undocumented attack-vulnerability links via the VULDAT tool.
AI.motivation: Cyber Threat Intelligence resources like MITRE ATT&CK and CVE have incomplete coverage of attack-vulnerability relationships, especially when attack descriptions appear before formal vulnerability linkages; this gap necessitates automated methods to infer vulnerabilities from textual attack data.
AI.method: Transformer-based sentence embedding models were used to encode attack and vulnerability descriptions into semantic vectors; similarity-based ranking was performed across 14 state-of-the-art models using four types of attack descriptions (Tactic, Technique, Procedure, Attack Pattern); the best-performing model was selected and integrated into the VULDAT tool.
AI.result: Technique-level descriptions in MITRE ATT&CK yielded the strongest predictive signal; the multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1 (MMPNet) model outperformed others due to its hybrid pre-training and semantic similarity optimization; the VULDAT tool successfully identified previously undocumented attack-vulnerability relationships and demonstrated generalization to real-world, unseen cyberattack reports.
AI.conclusion: Semantic similarity using transformer embeddings is effective for predicting vulnerabilities from attack descriptions; the approach enables proactive vulnerability management and enhances Cyber Threat Intelligence by uncovering missing links in existing knowledge bases.

title: Evaluating and Improving Automated Repository-Level Rust Issue Resolution with LLM-based Agents
comment: Accepted to the 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2026)
summary: The Rust programming language presents a steep learning curve and significant coding challenges, making the automation of issue resolution essential for its broader adoption. Recently, LLM-powered code agents have shown remarkable success in resolving complex software engineering tasks, yet their application to Rust has been limited by the absence of a large-scale, repository-level benchmark. To bridge this gap, we introduce Rust-SWE-bench, a benchmark comprising 500 real-world, repository-level software engineering tasks from 34 diverse and popular Rust repositories. We then perform a comprehensive study on Rust-SWE-bench with four representative agents and four state-of-the-art LLMs to establish a foundational understanding of their capabilities and limitations in the Rust ecosystem. Our extensive study reveals that while ReAct-style agents are promising, i.e., resolving up to 21.2% of issues, they are limited by two primary challenges: comprehending repository-wide code structure and complying with Rust's strict type and trait semantics. We also find that issue reproduction is rather critical for task resolution. Inspired by these findings, we propose RUSTFORGER, a novel agentic approach that integrates an automated test environment setup with a Rust metaprogramming-driven dynamic tracing strategy to facilitate reliable issue reproduction and dynamic analysis. The evaluation shows that RUSTFORGER using Claude-Sonnet-3.7 significantly outperforms all baselines, resolving 28.6% of tasks on Rust-SWE-bench, i.e., a 34.9% improvement over the strongest baseline, and, in aggregate, uniquely solves 46 tasks that no other agent could solve across all adopted advanced LLMs.

AI.tldr: Introduces Rust-SWE-bench, a repository-level benchmark with 500 real-world Rust tasks, and proposes RUSTFORGER, an agentic approach using dynamic tracing and automated test setup, achieving 28.6% task resolution, a 34.9% improvement over the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Rust's steep learning curve and complexity necessitate automated issue resolution; however, lack of a large-scale, repository-level benchmark limits progress in applying LLMs to Rust software engineering tasks.
AI.method: Proposes Rust-SWE-bench with 500 real-world tasks from 34 Rust repositories; evaluates four agents and four LLMs; introduces RUSTFORGER, which combines automated test environment setup with Rust metaprogramming-based dynamic tracing for improved issue reproduction and analysis.
AI.result: RUSTFORGER with Claude-Sonnet-3.7 achieves 28.6% task resolution on Rust-SWE-bench, outperforming the strongest baseline by 34.9% and uniquely solving 46 tasks unsolved by any other agent-LLM combination.
AI.conclusion: Effective Rust issue resolution requires reliable reproduction and understanding of type/traits and code structure; RUSTFORGER's integration of dynamic tracing and test automation significantly advances agent-based Rust development.

title: Differentially Private Data-Driven Markov Chain Modeling
summary: Markov chains model a wide range of user behaviors. However, generating accurate Markov chain models requires substantial user data, and sharing these models without privacy protections may reveal sensitive information about the underlying user data. We introduce a method for protecting user data used to formulate a Markov chain model. First, we develop a method for privatizing database queries whose outputs are elements of the unit simplex, and we prove that this method is differentially private. We quantify its accuracy by bounding the expected KL divergence between private and non-private queries. We extend this method to privatize stochastic matrices whose rows are each a simplex-valued query of a database, which includes data-driven Markov chain models. To assess their accuracy, we analytically bound the change in the stationary distribution and the change in the convergence rate between a non-private Markov chain model and its private form. Simulations show that under a typical privacy implementation, our method yields less than 2% error in the stationary distribution, indicating that our approach to private modeling faithfully captures the behavior of the systems we study.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a differentially private method to protect user data in data-driven Markov chain models by privatizing simplex-valued queries. The approach ensures strong privacy with minimal impact on model accuracy, demonstrated via bounded KL divergence, theoretical error bounds, and simulations showing less than 2% error in stationary distributions.
AI.motivation: Markov chain models require large user datasets, which may contain sensitive information. Direct sharing without privacy can lead to data leakage, necessitating a method that ensures privacy while maintaining model utility.
AI.method: A differentially private method is developed for privatizing simplex-valued database queries and extended to stochastic matrices in Markov chain models. Analytical bounds are derived for changes in stationary distribution and convergence rate; simulations validate accuracy.
AI.result: The method achieves less than 2% error in the stationary distribution under typical privacy parameters. Expected KL divergence is bounded, and analytical guarantees are provided for perturbation in both stationary distribution and convergence rate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method for privatizing Markov chain models using differential privacy preserves high accuracy while protecting user data, with minimal error in the stationary distribution under typical privacy settings.

title: Productivity and Collaboration in Hybrid Agile Teams: An Interview Study
summary: Hybrid work has become a reality post-pandemic, transforming how Agile teams deliver value, collaborate, and adapt. This study investigate how hybrid settings influence productivity and collaboration through nine interviews with three Norwegian Agile teams. Our findings show that hybrid work reduces informal interaction, creates uneven participation, and increases reliance on digital tools. Agile ceremonies became alignment anchors, while trust, communication, and tool support mediate team effectiveness. Hybrid Agile work is an evolving field that requires tailored structures to support inclusion, team cohesion, and sustainable performance.

AI.tldr: This study explores how hybrid work affects Agile teams through interviews with three Norwegian teams, revealing challenges in collaboration and participation, and highlighting the importance of Agile ceremonies and supportive structures for effective hybrid Agile work.
AI.motivation: The shift to hybrid work post-pandemic has transformed Agile team dynamics, necessitating an understanding of its effects on collaboration, productivity, and team adaptation.
AI.method: Nine interviews were conducted with three Norwegian Agile teams to investigate the impact of hybrid work on productivity and collaboration.
AI.result: Hybrid work reduces informal interaction, leads to uneven participation, increases dependence on digital tools, and makes Agile ceremonies critical for alignment; trust, communication, and tool support are key mediators of team effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid Agile work requires tailored structures to support inclusion, team cohesion, and sustainable performance due to reduced informal interaction, uneven participation, and increased reliance on digital tools.

title: Silent Egress: When Implicit Prompt Injection Makes LLM Agents Leak Without a Trace
summary: Agentic large language model systems increasingly automate tasks by retrieving URLs and calling external tools. We show that this workflow gives rise to implicit prompt injection: adversarial instructions embedded in automatically generated URL previews, including titles, metadata, and snippets, can introduce a system-level risk that we refer to as silent egress. Using a fully local and reproducible testbed, we demonstrate that a malicious web page can induce an agent to issue outbound requests that exfiltrate sensitive runtime context, even when the final response shown to the user appears harmless. In 480 experimental runs with a qwen2.5:7b-based agent, the attack succeeds with high probability (P (egress) =0.89), and 95% of successful attacks are not detected by output-based safety checks. We also introduce sharded exfiltration, where sensitive information is split across multiple requests to avoid detection. This strategy reduces single-request leakage metrics by 73% (Leak@1) and bypasses simple data loss prevention mechanisms. Our ablation results indicate that defenses applied at the prompt layer offer limited protection, while controls at the system and network layers, such as domain allowlisting and redirect-chain analysis, are considerably more effective. These findings suggest that network egress should be treated as a first-class security outcome in agentic LLM systems. We outline architectural directions, including provenance tracking and capability isolation, that go beyond prompt-level hardening.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes 'silent egress'—a system-level vulnerability in agentic LLMs where malicious URL previews enable undetected data exfiltration via implicit prompt injection. Using a qwen2.5:7b-based agent, the authors show 89% attack success, with 95% evading detection; sharding further reduces detectability. Effective mitigation requires system- and network-layer controls, not just prompt hardening.
AI.motivation: As agentic LLM systems increasingly retrieve URLs and invoke external tools autonomously, they become vulnerable to new attack vectors. The authors highlight 'silent egress'—undetected data exfiltration via seemingly benign outputs—as an emerging system-level threat stemming from implicit prompt injection in automatically ingested web content.
AI.method: The authors designed a reproducible, fully local testbed to evaluate implicit prompt injection via malicious URL previews. They tested a qwen2.5:7b-based agent across 480 runs, measuring egress success rates and evasion of output-based safety checks. They introduced 'sharded exfiltration'—splitting sensitive data across multiple requests—and evaluated detection bypass efficacy. Ablation studies assessed the effectiveness of various defensive layers.
AI.result: In 480 experiments, the attack achieved an 89% success rate in triggering unauthorized outbound requests, with 95% of successful exfiltrations evading output-based safety checks. Sharded exfiltration reduced single-request leakage by 73% (Leak@1) and effectively bypassed basic data loss prevention. Prompt-layer defenses showed limited efficacy, while system- and network-level controls (e.g., domain allowlisting, redirect-chain analysis) were significantly more effective.
AI.conclusion: Network egress must be treated as a critical security outcome in agentic LLM systems, requiring system- and network-layer defenses such as domain allowlisting, provenance tracking, and capability isolation rather than relying solely on prompt-level safeguards.

title: Managing Uncertainty in LLM-based Multi-Agent System Operation
summary: Applying LLM-based multi-agent software systems in safety-critical domains such as lifespan echocardiography introduces system-level risks that cannot be addressed by improving model accuracy alone. During system operation, beyond individual LLM behavior, uncertainty propagates through agent coordination, data pipelines, human-in-the-loop interaction, and runtime control logic. Yet existing work largely treats uncertainty at the model level rather than as a first-class software engineering concern. This paper approaches uncertainty from both system-level and runtime perspectives. We first differentiate epistemological and ontological uncertainties in the context of LLM-based multi-agent software system operation. Building on this foundation, we propose a lifecycle-based uncertainty management framework comprising four mechanisms: representation, identification, evolution, and adaptation. The uncertainty lifecycle governs how uncertainties emerge, transform, and are mitigated across architectural layers and execution phases, enabling structured runtime governance and controlled adaptation. We demonstrate the feasibility of the framework using a real-world LLM-based multi-agent echocardiographic software system developed in clinical collaboration, showing improved reliability and diagnosability in diagnostic reasoning. The proposed approach generalizes to other safety-critical LLM-based multi-agent software systems, supporting principled operational control and runtime assurance beyond model-centric methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lifecycle-based uncertainty management framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems in safety-critical domains, distinguishing epistemic and ontological uncertainties and demonstrating improved system reliability and diagnosability in a clinical echocardiography application.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches focus on model-level uncertainty, but safety-critical LLM-based multi-agent systems face system-level risks arising from agent coordination, data pipelines, human interaction, and runtime logic. These require treating uncertainty as a first-class software engineering concern.
AI.method: The paper introduces a framework with four mechanisms—representation, identification, evolution, and adaptation—to manage uncertainty across the system lifecycle. It differentiates between epistemic and ontological uncertainties and applies the framework to a real-world LLM-based multi-agent echocardiographic system developed in clinical collaboration.
AI.result: Application of the framework in a real-world echocardiographic system demonstrated improved reliability and diagnosability in diagnostic reasoning, validating the feasibility and effectiveness of the lifecycle-based uncertainty management approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lifecycle-based uncertainty management framework provides a structured approach to handling uncertainty in LLM-based multi-agent systems, enhancing reliability and diagnosability in safety-critical applications like echocardiography, and generalizes beyond model-centric methods to support principled runtime assurance.

title: Explainability-Aware Evaluation of Transfer Learning Models for IoT DDoS Detection Under Resource Constraints
summary: Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks threaten the availability of Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures, particularly under resource-constrained deployment conditions. Although transfer learning models have shown promising detection accuracy, their reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in operational environments remain insufficiently explored. This study presents an explainability-aware empirical evaluation of seven pre-trained convolutional neural network architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection using the CICDDoS2019 dataset and an image-based traffic representation. The analysis integrates performance metrics, reliability-oriented statistics (MCC, Youden Index, confidence intervals), latency and training cost assessment, and interpretability evaluation using Grad-CAM and SHAP. Results indicate that DenseNet and MobileNet-based architectures achieve strong detection performance while demonstrating superior reliability and compact, class-consistent attribution patterns. DenseNet169 offers the strongest reliability and interpretability alignment, whereas MobileNetV3 provides an effective latency-accuracy trade-off for fog-level deployment. The findings emphasize the importance of combining performance, reliability, and explainability criteria when selecting deep learning models for IoT DDoS detection.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates seven pre-trained CNNs for IoT DDoS detection using image-represented traffic data, emphasizing performance, reliability, and interpretability. DenseNet169 and MobileNetV3 emerge as top choices for reliable and efficient deployment in IoT environments.
AI.motivation: Despite high detection accuracy of transfer learning models in IoT DDoS detection, their reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in operational, resource-constrained environments remain under-investigated. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating models not only on performance but also on reliability and explainability, which are crucial for trust and deployment in real-world IoT systems.
AI.method: The authors conducted an explainability-aware empirical evaluation of seven pre-trained CNN architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection. Traffic data from the CICDDoS2019 dataset was transformed into images for CNN input. Evaluation included performance metrics, reliability measures (MCC, Youden Index, confidence intervals), latency and training cost analysis, and interpretability assessment using Grad-CAM and SHAP.
AI.result: DenseNet and MobileNet-based models achieved high detection performance with superior reliability and consistent interpretability. DenseNet169 showed the best alignment between reliability and interpretability, while MobileNetV3 offered the best trade-off between latency and accuracy, making it suitable for fog computing environments. Compact and class-consistent attribution patterns were observed in top-performing models.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that DenseNet and MobileNet-based architectures, particularly DenseNet169 and MobileNetV3, are well-suited for IoT DDoS detection due to their strong performance, reliability, and interpretability. DenseNet169 excels in reliability and explanation consistency, while MobileNetV3 is optimal for latency-sensitive fog environments. The integration of performance, reliability, and explainability is critical in model selection for real-world IoT security applications.

title: CL4SE: A Context Learning Benchmark For Software Engineering Tasks
summary: Context engineering has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for unlocking the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Software Engineering (SE) tasks, enabling performance gains at test time without model fine-tuning. Despite its success, existing research lacks a systematic taxonomy of SE-specific context types and a dedicated benchmark to quantify the heterogeneous effects of different contexts across core SE workflows. To address this gap, we propose CL4SE (Context Learning for Software Engineering), a comprehensive benchmark featuring a fine-grained taxonomy of four SE-oriented context types (interpretable examples, project-specific context, procedural decision-making context, and positive & negative context), each mapped to a representative task (code generation, code summarization, code review, and patch correctness assessment). We construct high-quality datasets comprising over 13,000 samples from more than 30 open-source projects and evaluate five mainstream LLMs across nine metrics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that context learning yields an average performance improvement of 24.7% across all tasks. Specifically, procedural context boosts code review performance by up to 33% (Qwen3-Max), mixed positive-negative context improves patch assessment by 30% (DeepSeek-V3), project-specific context increases code summarization BLEU by 14.78% (GPT-Oss-120B), and interpretable examples enhance code generation PASS@1 by 5.72% (DeepSeek-V3). CL4SE establishes the first standardized evaluation framework for SE context learning, provides actionable empirical insights into task-specific context design, and releases a large-scale dataset to facilitate reproducible research in this domain.

AI.tldr: CL4SE introduces a structured benchmark for context learning in Software Engineering, proposing a four-type taxonomy and evaluating context effects on major SE tasks using 13,000+ samples from open-source projects, showing significant performance gains across five LLMs.
AI.motivation: Despite the success of context engineering in improving LLM performance for Software Engineering tasks, there is a lack of systematic categorization of SE-specific context types and a dedicated benchmark to assess their impact across different SE workflows.
AI.method: The authors propose CL4SE, a benchmark with a fine-grained taxonomy of four SE-specific context types—interpretable examples, project-specific context, procedural decision-making context, and positive & negative context—each aligned with a representative SE task. They construct a dataset of over 13,000 samples from 30+ open-source projects and evaluate five mainstream LLMs across nine metrics.
AI.result: Context learning improves LLM performance by an average of 24.7% across tasks. Procedural context increases code review performance by up to 33% (Qwen3-Max), mixed positive-negative context improves patch correctness assessment by 30% (DeepSeek-V3), project-specific context boosts code summarization BLEU by 14.78% (GPT-Oss-120B), and interpretable examples enhance code generation PASS@1 by 5.72% (DeepSeek-V3).
AI.conclusion: CL4SE establishes the first standardized evaluation framework for context learning in Software Engineering, offering a reproducible benchmark, empirical insights into task-specific context effectiveness, and a publicly released large-scale dataset to advance research in LLM-based SE applications.

title: Systems-Level Attack Surface of Edge Agent Deployments on IoT
summary: Edge deployment of LLM agents on IoT hardware introduces attack surfaces absent from cloud-hosted orchestration. We present an empirical security analysis of three architectures (cloud-hosted, edge-local swarm, and hybrid) using a multi-device home-automation testbed with local MQTT messaging and an Android smartphone as an edge inference node. We identify five systems-level attack surfaces, including two emergent failures observed during live testbed operation: coordination-state divergence and induced trust erosion. We frame core security properties as measurable systems metrics: data egress volume, failover window exposure, sovereignty boundary integrity, and provenance chain completeness. Our measurements show that edge-local deployments eliminate routine cloud data exposure but silently degrade sovereignty when fallback mechanisms trigger, with boundary crossings invisible at the application layer. Provenance chains remain complete under cooperative operation yet are trivially bypassed without cryptographic enforcement. Failover windows create transient blind spots exploitable for unauthorised actuation. These results demonstrate that deployment architecture, not just model or prompt design, is a primary determinant of security risk in agent-controlled IoT systems.

AI.tldr: Edge deployment of LLM agents on IoT devices introduces new security risks; this paper evaluates three architectures (cloud, edge-local, hybrid) in a home-automated testbed, identifying key attack surfaces and proposing measurable security metrics.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on edge/IoT devices, expanding the attack surface beyond cloud systems; understanding architectural security implications is critical for secure deployment.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of three LLM agent architectures (cloud-hosted, edge-local swarm, hybrid) using a multi-device home-automation testbed with local MQTT and an Android smartphone as edge node; identification of attack surfaces and definition of measurable security metrics.
AI.result: Identified five systems-level attack surfaces, including coordination-state divergence and induced trust erosion; edge-local deployments prevent cloud data exposure but risk silent sovereignty degradation during fallbacks; provenance chains lack cryptographic enforcement and are easily bypassed; failover windows enable unauthorized actuation.
AI.conclusion: Deployment architecture is a primary factor in security risk for LLM-agent-controlled IoT systems, more so than just model or prompt design; architectural choices must be evaluated through systems-level security metrics.

title: LLM-Powered Silent Bug Fuzzing in Deep Learning Libraries via Versatile and Controlled Bug Transfer
summary:
Deep learning (DL) libraries are widely used in critical applications, where even subtle silent bugs can lead to serious consequences. While existing DL fuzzing techniques have made progress in detecting crashes, they inherently struggle to detect silent bugs due to the lack of effective test programs and corresponding oracles.
  Building on the observation that historical bug reports contain rich, underutilized information about silent bugs, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to perform versatile yet controlled bug transfer for silent bug fuzzing. Specifically, our approach uses LLMs to extract context-aware bug patterns from historical issues, match semantically related Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) using functionality-based embeddings, and synthesize test cases with customized oracles. This enables proactive detection of silent bugs by transferring high-risk contexts and oracle designs from known buggy APIs to functionally similar target APIs. To ensure the reliability of our context-aware bug transfer, we introduce an LLM-powered self-validation module that systematically evaluates the validity of each transferred bug instance. We implement this methodology in a tool named TransFuzz and evaluate it on three mainstream DL libraries: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and MindSpore.
